pos: v. (to bring the hand or body into contact with; rendering Hebrew naga, Greek haptomai)
etymology: From French toucher, to feel or handle. Under the law touch was a category of defilement; in the Gospels the direction reverses, for what our Lord touches is not made unclean but made clean.
biblical_def: Touch in Scripture is rarely incidental; it transfers something. Under the law contact with the unclean defiled the one who touched, and the seraph's touch at Isaiah's call shows the principle working the other way by divine act: “And he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged” (Isaiah 6:7). A live coal from the altar touches the unclean lips and the uncleanness goes, because the coal comes from the place of sacrifice. The Gospels press the reversal further. A leper, whom no one might touch and who might touch no one, is met by a hand: “And Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed” (Matthew 8:3). Christ is not defiled by the contact; the leper is cleansed by it. Yet the word keeps its warning edge for those who would walk with God: “come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you” (2 Corinthians 6:17). And the same Apostle turns the word against invented holiness, quoting the ascetics' rule in order to condemn it — “Touch not; taste not; handle not” (Colossians 2:21) — because commandments of men cannot cleanse what only Christ's touch can.
webster_summary: To come in contact with; to perceive by feeling; to affect; to meddle with. Scripture uses touch for defilement under the law, for cleansing at Christ's hand, for separation from what is unclean, and for the man-made rules that only appear to be holiness.
webster_full: TOUCH, v.t. [Fr. toucher; It. toccare.] To come in contact with; to hit or strike against; to extend to so as to have no space between.
2. To perceive by the sense of feeling; to feel.
3. To meddle with; to handle; as, touch not that vessel.
4. To affect; to move; to melt; as, a tale that touches the heart.
5. To relate to; to concern; as, this matter touches the interest of the state.
TOUCH, n. Contact; the act of touching; the sense of feeling, or the organ by which contact is perceived; also, a slight essay or trial; as, the touch of a master.
scriptures: And he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged.
And Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
corruption_summary: The word is pulled to two opposite errors: an asceticism that multiplies rules about what may not be touched, and a worldliness that denies there is anything a Christian must not touch at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 2:21 is one of the most misquoted verses in the English Bible, because Paul is not issuing the rule but quoting it. “Touch not; taste not; handle not” is the slogan of the false teachers at Colosse, and the Apostle's judgment on such ordinances is that they have a shew of wisdom and are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh. Where a church builds its identity on a list of untouchables — foods, drinks, days, associations invented rather than commanded — it has not achieved holiness; it has exchanged the commandments of God for the traditions of men, and the exchange always flatters the man keeping the list.

The opposite corruption reads the Apostle's freedom as if it dissolved every boundary, so that 2 Corinthians 6:17 is treated as an antique scruple. But the command to touch not the unclean thing is not a food rule; its context is the unequal yoke, and the promise attached to it is that God will receive His people. The distinction the age cannot hold is the one Scripture holds easily: God has commanded real separations, and men have invented false ones, and the remedy for the invented sort is never the abolition of the commanded sort. Christ's own touch settles the matter — He was never defiled by the leper, and He never treated uncleanness as nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew naga (to touch, reach, strike) governs the purity laws and the seraph's coal; Greek haptomai (to fasten to, touch) is the Gospels' word for the touch that heals, and thinganō (to handle) the word of the ascetics' rule.
roots_lines: Hebrew naga (H5060) — to touch, reach, strike; the verb of the purity laws and of the coal that touched Isaiah's lips.
Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be or become unclean; the state that touching the unclean transferred under the law.
Greek haptomai (G680) — to fasten to, to touch; used of our Lord touching the leper and of the woman touching His garment.
Greek thinganō (G2345) — to handle, to touch; the verb in the ascetic slogan Paul quotes at Colossians 2:21.
Greek akathartos (G169) — unclean, impure; the thing the separated are commanded not to touch.
usage: “Lo, this hath touched thy lips” — the coal from the altar cleanses what it touches.
“Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him” — Christ takes the leper's place without taking his defilement.
“Touch not; taste not; handle not” — Paul quotes the rule of men in order to condemn it.

pos: v. (to push or drive with force; to stab; rendering Hebrew dachah, garash, Greek ekballo, ballo)
etymology: From the Norse thrysta, to press or force. The word carries violence in every direction it points: men thrust at the righteous, God thrusts the impenitent out, and Thomas is told to thrust his hand into a wounded side.
biblical_def: To thrust is to move a thing by sudden force, and Scripture uses it for the sharpest actions on both sides of the judgment. Our Lord applies it to the exclusion of the presumptuous: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out” (Luke 13:28). The grief there is not ignorance but sight — they see the patriarchs within — and the verb is violent because the exclusion is decisive. The Psalmist knows the word from the receiving end and answers it with the LORD's help: “Thou hast thrust sore at me that I might fall: but the LORD helped me” (Psalm 118:13). Even Pharaoh's hardened resistance ends in a thrusting that serves God's purpose: “when he shall let you go, he shall surely thrust you out hence altogether” (Exodus 11:1). The most tender use is also the most physical. To a disciple who would not believe the resurrection on testimony, the risen Christ offers His body as evidence: “reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing” (John 20:27). The wounds are real enough to be handled, which is the point.
webster_summary: To push or drive with force; to shove; to stab or pierce; to expel or force out. Scripture uses it of the impenitent thrust from the kingdom, of the enemy's violent push, and of the hand Thomas was told to thrust into the risen Saviour's side.
webster_full: THRUST, v.t. [L. trudo; Norm. thrysta, to press.] To push or drive with force; to shove; to impel; to urge.
2. To stab; to pierce with a pointed weapon; as, to thrust a sword through the body.
3. To obtrude; to intrude; to push in or into; as, to thrust one's self into a crowd.
4. To expel; to drive out or away; as, to thrust out an enemy.
THRUST, v.i. To make a push; to attack with a pointed weapon; to intrude; to squeeze in.
THRUST, n. A violent push or driving, as with a pointed weapon; an attack; an assault.
scriptures: There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out.
Thou hast thrust sore at me that I might fall: but the LORD helped me.

And the LORD said unto Moses, Yet will I bring one plague more upon Pharaoh, and upon Egypt; afterwards he will let you go hence: when he shall let you go, he shall surely thrust you out hence altogether.
Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.
corruption_summary: Doubt has been promoted from a weakness Christ corrected into a virtue the church celebrates — so that “be not faithless, but believing” is read as an endorsement of the questioning it plainly rebukes.
corruption_paragraphs: Thomas is now regularly held up as the patron of honest doubt, and the scene in John 20 is retold as our Lord's blessing upon a questioning temperament. The text says otherwise. Christ grants the evidence and then rebukes the state that demanded it — be not faithless — and immediately pronounces the greater blessing on those who have not seen and yet have believed. Doubt is treated in Scripture as a thing to be helped, healed, and repented of, never as a mark of maturity. A church that teaches otherwise has made a virtue of the very condition the risen Lord came into the room to end.

The same passage rebukes an opposite error. Because Thomas was permitted to handle the wounds, the resurrection cannot be reduced to a spiritual impression on the disciples, an abiding influence, or the survival of the cause. A body with handleable wounds is either there or it is not. Luke 13:28 keeps the other end of the doctrine standing: there is an inside and an outside to the kingdom, and men may be thrust out of it. Both halves are unpopular, and both are the plain sense of the words.
roots_summary: Hebrew dachah (to push, thrust, cast down) and garash (to drive out) carry the Old Testament sense; Greek ekballo (to cast out) and ballo (to throw, put) render the thrusting out and the thrusting in.
roots_lines: Hebrew dachah (H1760) — to push, thrust, cast down; the enemy's violent push in Psalm 118:13.
Hebrew garash (H1644) — to drive out, expel; used of Pharaoh thrusting Israel out of Egypt.
Greek ekballo (G1544) — to cast out, thrust out; the verb of exclusion from the kingdom in Luke 13:28.
Greek ballo (G906) — to throw, cast, put; used of Thomas putting his hand into the Saviour's side.
Greek apistos (G571) — faithless, unbelieving; the condition our Lord names and forbids in John 20:27.
usage: “You yourselves thrust out” — exclusion from the kingdom is decisive and is seen by those excluded.
“Thou hast thrust sore at me” — the violence is real and the LORD's help is greater.
“Thrust it into my side: and be not faithless” — evidence is granted and unbelief is rebuked in one breath.

pos: v. (to separate into parts; to distinguish rightly; rendering Hebrew badal, chatsah, Greek orthotomeo, merizo)
etymology: From Latin divido, to part or separate. Creation itself begins with dividings, and the Bible treats the ability to divide rightly — light from darkness, holy from profane, law from gospel — as a mark of wisdom rather than of a quarrelsome spirit.
biblical_def: Divide is a creation word before it is a controversial one. God's first recorded act upon the light is a separation: “And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness” (Genesis 1:4). Order in the world begins with things being set apart from one another, and the priests were later charged to put difference between holy and unholy on the same pattern. In redemption the word describes the making of a way where there was none: “lift thou up thy rod, and stretch out thine hand over the sea, and divide it: and the children of Israel shall go on dry ground through the midst of the sea” (Exodus 14:16). What divides the sea saves the people. Applied to the ministry of the word, dividing becomes the labourer's central skill: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). The figure is of cutting straight — a right cut rather than a ragged one. And Scripture itself does the dividing when it is preached: it is “sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12).
webster_summary: To part or separate into two or more pieces; to distribute; to distinguish or discriminate. Scripture makes dividing a creational act, a redemptive one at the sea, and the preacher's duty in handling the word of truth.
webster_full: DIVIDE, v.t. [L. divido; di and the root of video, to part.] To part or separate an entire thing; to part a thing into two or more pieces.
2. To cause to be separate; to keep apart by a partition or by an imaginary line; as, a wall divides two houses.
3. To make partition of, among a number; to deal out; to distribute; as, to divide an estate among heirs.
4. To disunite in opinion or interest; to make discordant.
5. To separate and distinguish; to discriminate; as, to divide truth from error.
DIVIDE, v.i. To part; to open; to cleave; also, to break friendship or agreement.
scriptures: And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness.
But lift thou up thy rod, and stretch out thine hand over the sea, and divide it: and the children of Israel shall go on dry ground through the midst of the sea.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
corruption_summary: Two errors run opposite ways: a flattening that treats all distinction-making as divisiveness, and an over-carving that slices the Scriptures into dispensations the confessions never knew.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning error is that dividing is itself a sin. To distinguish law from gospel, holy from profane, truth from error, sheep from wolves, is described as a failure of charity, and the man who makes such distinctions is charged with causing division. But 2 Timothy 2:15 makes right dividing the very definition of the approved workman, and Genesis 1:4 shows that separation is how God brings order out of what was without form. The alternative to dividing rightly is not unity; it is confusion, in which nothing can be affirmed because nothing has been distinguished from its opposite.

The opposite corruption over-divides. Dispensational schemes following Darby and Scofield carve the Scriptures into separate economies with separate peoples and separate programmes, until law and gospel, Israel and the church, are not distinguished but severed — a nineteenth-century novelty that no Reformation confession contains. Right dividing cuts straight along the seams Scripture itself provides: the covenants of works and grace, the promise and its fulfilment, the letter that kills and the Spirit that gives life. A cut that separates what God has joined is as ragged as a refusal to cut at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew badal (to separate, make a difference) governs the creation and priestly distinctions; chatsah (to cut in two) the dividing of the sea; Greek orthotomeo (to cut straight) is the workman's word in 2 Timothy 2:15.
roots_lines: Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, separate, make a difference; used of light from darkness and of the priests putting difference between holy and profane.
Hebrew chatsah (H2673) — to divide, to cut in two; used of the dividing of the waters at the Red Sea.
Hebrew baqa (H1234) — to cleave, split open; the stronger verb for the sea being broken apart.
Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, to handle rightly; the single-word command of 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek merismos (G3311) — a division, a dividing asunder; the word's work upon soul and spirit in Hebrews 4:12.
usage: “God divided the light from the darkness” — order in creation begins with separation.
“Rightly dividing the word of truth” — the figure is of a straight cut, not a ragged one.
“The dividing asunder of soul and spirit” — Scripture divides the man who reads it.

pos: v. (to extend or reach out at length; rendering Hebrew natah, Greek ekteino)
etymology: From Saxon streccan, to extend. The stretched-out arm is the Bible's standing figure for God's power exerted in redemption, and the stretched-out hand for His patience refused.
biblical_def: To stretch is to extend to full reach, and Scripture puts the figure to three great uses. The first is redemptive power. The LORD stakes His name upon it at the exodus: “I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments” (Exodus 6:6). The arm at full extension is deliverance at full strength, and the phrase becomes shorthand for the exodus ever after. The second use is creational, and its scale is deliberately domestic: it is He “that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in” (Isaiah 40:22). The heavens that overwhelm a man are handled by God as easily as a woman handles cloth. The third use is the stretched-out hand of invitation, and it carries the pathos of refusal: “Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded” (Proverbs 1:24). Wisdom's hand is out and unheeded. Our Lord takes the same verb into a miracle of obedience, where the command and the power come together: “Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it forth; and it was restored whole, like as the other” (Matthew 12:13).
webster_summary: To extend or draw out to greater length or breadth; to reach forth; to spread. Scripture uses the stretched-out arm for God's redeeming power, the stretched-out heavens for His ease in creating, and the stretched-out hand for mercy offered and refused.
webster_full: STRETCH, v.t. [Sax. streccan, to extend.] To draw out to greater length; to extend in a line; as, to stretch a cord or a rope.
2. To extend in breadth; to spread; as, to stretch cloth.
3. To reach forth; to put forth; as, to stretch out the hand.
4. To strain; to exaggerate; as, to stretch the truth.
5. To extend or spread over; as, a plain stretching to the sea.
STRETCH, n. Extension; reach; utmost extent of meaning or power; as, the stretch of the imagination; a stretch of authority.
scriptures: Wherefore say unto the children of Israel, I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments:
It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in:
Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded;
Then saith he to the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it forth; and it was restored whole, like as the other.
corruption_summary: The stretched-out arm has been demoted to poetry — a figure for inspiration or moral influence — where Scripture means an actual power that actually delivered a people out of an actual bondage.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the exodus is reclassified as national legend, the stretched-out arm becomes a metaphor for a people's aspiration and God is left with no arm at all. The phrase does not survive that treatment, because it was never decorative: Exodus 6:6 puts it inside a covenant promise with a named oppressor, a named people, and great judgments that fell in a particular year. Scripture reasons from that deliverance to every later one, and Israel is commanded to rehearse it to children as a fact. A God whose arm is a figure of speech cannot be appealed to when the next bondage comes.

The second flattening is subtler and touches Isaiah 40:22. Modern devotion often uses the stretched-out heavens to make man feel small and stops there, as though the point were our insignificance. The prophet's point is the reverse: he is comforting a people who thought their way was hid from the LORD, and the vastness of the heavens is offered as evidence that One who spreads them like a tent-cloth is not overtaxed by their case. Recover the argument and the figure does its proper work — the arm that stretched to redeem is the hand that stretches out still, and the tragedy of Proverbs 1:24 is that it can be ignored.
roots_summary: Hebrew natah (to stretch out, extend, incline) supplies both the outstretched arm of redemption and the stretched heavens; Greek ekteino (to extend, stretch forth) is the Gospels' word for the hand put forth at Christ's command.
roots_lines: Hebrew natah (H5186) — to stretch out, extend, incline; used of the outstretched arm, the stretched heavens, and a heart inclined.
Hebrew zerowa (H2220) — arm, strength; the member stretched out in Exodus 6:6 and the standing figure of divine power.
Hebrew doq (H1852) — a thin curtain, gauze; the fabric to which Isaiah 40:22 compares the heavens.
Greek ekteino (G1614) — to stretch forth, extend; the command and the obedience in Matthew 12:13.
Greek ephaploō — to spread out upon; the sense behind spreading the heavens as a tent to dwell in.
usage: “I will redeem you with a stretched out arm” — redemption is power at full extension.
“Stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain” — the scale that overwhelms man is handled by God like cloth.
“I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded” — mercy offered may be refused.

pos: v. (to look through in order to find; to examine thoroughly; rendering Hebrew chaqar, Greek ereunao)
etymology: From Old French cerchier, Latin circare, to go about. Scripture's searching runs both ways: God searches the heart that no man can read, and man is commanded to search the Scriptures that read him.
biblical_def: Search means to examine thoroughly rather than to glance, and Scripture makes God the first and most searching searcher. He claims the office as His own: “I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings” (Jeremiah 17:10). The verse follows immediately upon the declaration that the heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked, and who can know it — the answer being that God can, and does. The believer's proper response is not concealment but invitation: “Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts” (Psalm 139:23). A man who has hidden nothing has nothing to lose by the searching. The Spirit's searching reaches further still, into God Himself: “the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10), which is why the things freely given to us can be known at all. Turned toward the text, the verb becomes a command with a warning attached, for searching may be done wrongly: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (John 5:39). Men may search diligently and miss the One the search is about.
webster_summary: To look over or through for the purpose of finding; to examine; to probe or explore. Scripture applies the word to God searching the heart, the Spirit searching the deep things of God, and men commanded to search the Scriptures that testify of Christ.
webster_full: SEARCH, v.t. [Fr. chercher; L. circare, to go about.] To look over or through, for the purpose of finding something; to explore; to examine by inspection.
2. To inquire; to seek for; to look for; as, to search out the cause.
3. To probe; as, to search a wound.
4. To examine; to try; as, to search the heart.
SEARCH, v.i. To seek; to look for; to make inquiry; to make examination.
SEARCH, n. The act of seeking or looking for something; inquiry; examination; a seeking or looking for.
scriptures: I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.
Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:
But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit: for the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God.
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
corruption_summary: Searching the Scriptures has been recast as a hunt for whatever a reader finds meaningful, so that the text yields a private message rather than testifying of Christ and searching the reader.
corruption_paragraphs: The common modern method reverses the direction of the searching. A man comes to the text to find what it means to him, and the question of what it means is quietly retired. But John 5:39 was spoken to the most diligent searchers of their generation, men who knew the text and missed its subject, and our Lord's complaint is precisely that their searching terminated on itself. Scripture has an object, and the object is a Person; a search that does not arrive there has failed however industrious it was. Hebrews and the Psalms add the further point that the reader is not the examiner but the examined.

A second corruption runs opposite and is more respectable: the notion that the heart is finally unsearchable even by God — that motives are so tangled that no verdict on them is possible, and therefore none should be pronounced. Jeremiah 17:10 forecloses it. The heart is unsearchable by man, which is exactly why the LORD reserves the searching to Himself and renders to every man according to his ways. The believer's comfort is not that his heart escapes examination but that he may invite the Examiner, as David does, and be searched by One who has already provided a righteousness not his own.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaqar (to search out, examine) and bachan (to try, test as metal) supply the Old Testament sense; Greek ereunao (to search, examine) is used both of the Spirit searching the deep things of God and of men searching the Scriptures.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out, examine thoroughly; used of searching a land, a matter, and a heart.
Hebrew bachan (H974) — to try, prove, test as a refiner tests metal; the trying of the reins in Jeremiah 17:10.
Hebrew kilyah (H3629) — reins, kidneys; the seat of the inward affections that God tries.
Greek ereunao (G2045) — to search, examine into; used of the Spirit and of the command in John 5:39.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to judge; the Berean word for examining the Scriptures daily.
usage: “I the LORD search the heart” — what is unsearchable to man is open to God.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart” — the believer invites the examination he cannot escape.
“They are they which testify of me” — a search that misses Christ has missed the point of the book.

pos: v. (to destroy or use up entirely; rendering Hebrew kalah, 'akal, Greek analisko, dapanao)
etymology: From Latin consumo, to take up wholly. Scripture's consuming is chiefly God's: a fire that is His own nature, before which His people are preserved and against which nothing unholy stands.
biblical_def: To consume is to use up entirely, leaving nothing, and Scripture's primary use makes the consuming a divine attribute rather than a divine mood: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29). The words are quoted out of Deuteronomy into a passage about a kingdom which cannot be moved, so that the fire is set beside grace rather than against it. Precisely because that is what God is, the preservation of sinners requires an explanation, and Scripture gives two. The first is mercy: “It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not” (Lamentations 3:22). The prophet is sitting in the ruins of Jerusalem when he says it, which is the strongest possible setting for the claim. The second is immutability: “For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed” (Malachi 3:6). The people's survival rests on God's unchangeableness, not on their improvement. The word turns downward when men do the consuming, and James names the misuse exactly: “Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts” (James 4:3). Prayer offered so that appetite may be fed is prayer aimed at consumption.
webster_summary: To destroy by separating the parts; to burn up; to waste; to spend or use entirely. Scripture calls God a consuming fire, grounds His people's survival in His mercy and immutability, and warns of prayers offered only to feed appetite.
webster_full: CONSUME, v.t. [L. consumo; con and sumo, to take.] To destroy by separating the parts of a thing, by decomposition, as by fire, or eating; to burn up; to devour.
2. To waste; to squander; to spend; as, to consume an estate.
3. To spend; to cause to pass away, as time; as, to consume the day in idleness.
4. To destroy; to bring to utter ruin; to exterminate.
CONSUME, v.i. To waste away slowly; to be exhausted; to perish; as, the body consumes by sickness.
CONSUMING, ppr. Burning up; wasting; destroying; expending.
scriptures: For our God is a consuming fire.
It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.
corruption_summary: The consuming fire has been enlisted for annihilationism — the claim that the lost are burned out of existence — and, in the opposite direction, softened until God's holiness threatens nothing at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Annihilationism takes the language of consuming and destruction as proof that the punishment of the wicked ends in extinction rather than in conscious suffering. The argument cannot carry the texts. Our Lord uses the same breath for the life and the punishment, everlasting in both directions (Matthew 25:46), and Revelation describes torment that ascends for ever and ever. Hebrews 12:29 is not describing the fate of the lost at all; it is a motive for reverence addressed to the church that receives an unshakable kingdom. The doctrine of eternal conscious punishment is the historic Christian position, and the confessions state it because Scripture does.

The commoner error runs the other way, keeping the word and removing its edge, so that God's holiness is a warmth rather than a fire and no one need serve Him with reverence and godly fear. Lamentations 3:22 loses everything under that treatment. If nothing was ever owed, mercy is not mercy, and Jeremiah's wonder in the ruins is sentimentality. Hold both together as Scripture does: God is a consuming fire; His people are not consumed; and the reason lies in His compassions and His unchangeableness, never in the diminishing of the fire.
roots_summary: Hebrew kalah (to complete, finish, consume) and 'akal (to eat, devour) supply the Old Testament sense; Greek analisko (to use up) and dapanao (to spend, consume) render the wasting and the spending.
roots_lines: Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to complete, to finish, to consume; the verb of Lamentations 3:22 and Malachi 3:6.
Hebrew 'akal (H398) — to eat, to devour; used of fire eating up what it burns.
Hebrew 'esh (H784) — fire; the element in which the LORD appeared at Sinai and which Hebrews applies to His nature.
Greek katanalisko (G2654) — to consume utterly; the participle in “a consuming fire” at Hebrews 12:29.
Greek dapanao (G1159) — to spend, to consume; the verb of James 4:3 for spending an answer upon lusts.
usage: “Our God is a consuming fire” — the fire is what God is, not merely what He does when provoked.
“It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed” — survival is credited to compassion, not to merit.
“That ye may consume it upon your lusts” — prayer aimed at appetite is prayer amiss.

pos: v. (to mix or blend together; rendering Hebrew 'arab, macak, Greek mignumi)
etymology: From Saxon mengan, to mix. Scripture watches mingling closely, because a people set apart is undone not usually by conquest but by blending, and because the cup a man is given is said to be mingled by another hand.
biblical_def: To mingle is to mix things until they are no longer distinct, and Scripture treats the act as morally weighted. Israel's decline is summed up in a single verse of mixture: “But were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works” (Psalm 106:35). The order is instructive — mingling came first and learning followed, because practice is caught before it is chosen. Daniel uses the word for a political union that cannot hold: “they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men: but they shall not cleave one to another, even as iron is not mixed with clay” (Daniel 2:43). Some things may be mingled and still refuse to bond. Wisdom, by contrast, mingles deliberately and hospitably: “She hath killed her beasts; she hath mingled her wine; she hath also furnished her table” (Proverbs 9:2), where the mingling is preparation for a feast to which the simple are invited. The word reaches its darkest use at the cross, where a drugged cup is offered and refused: “They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall: and when he had tasted thereof, he would not drink” (Matthew 27:34). Our Lord tasted enough to know what it was and declined the dulling of His sufferings.
webster_summary: To mix; to blend; to unite so that the parts are no longer distinct; to join in company. Scripture uses it of Israel mingled among the heathen, of unions that will not bond, of Wisdom's prepared wine, and of the cup our Lord refused at Golgotha.
webster_full: MINGLE, v.t. [Sax. mengan, to mix.] To mix; to blend; to unite in one body; as, to mingle liquors of different kinds.
2. To mix or blend without order or promiscuously; to confuse.
3. To compound; to make by mixing ingredients; as, to mingle a potion.
4. To join in mutual intercourse or in society; as, to mingle with a crowd.
MINGLE, v.i. To be mixed or united; to be joined; as, oil will not mingle with water.
MINGLE, n. A mixture; a medley; a promiscuous mass.
scriptures: But were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works.
And whereas thou sawest iron mixed with miry clay, they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men: but they shall not cleave one to another, even as iron is not mixed with clay.
She hath killed her beasts; she hath mingled her wine; she hath also furnished her table.
They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall: and when he had tasted thereof, he would not drink.
corruption_summary: Syncretism is now defended as breadth: the church is urged to mingle its doctrine with the surrounding religion of the age, and the mingling is called generosity rather than what Psalm 106 calls it.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 106:35 describes how a covenant people actually falls. Not by decree or by conquest, but by association that becomes imitation — they were mingled, and then they learned. The pattern holds. Where a church takes the moral vocabulary, the anthropology, and the aims of the surrounding culture into its own preaching and calls the result relevance, doctrine is not usually denied outright; it is diluted until it can no longer be distinguished from what the age already believed. The psalm's verdict on the process is not that it was unwise but that it was idolatry, and it names the outcome plainly in the verses that follow.

Daniel 2:43 supplies the corrective observation. Some mixtures will not hold however forcibly they are pressed together; iron and clay stay iron and clay. The gospel and the religion of the age are that sort of pairing, which is why every generation's attempt to fuse them produces a thing that cannot bear weight and does not last a generation. Recover the older instinct: the church is to be in the world and unmingled with it, hospitable as Wisdom is hospitable in Proverbs 9, and clear-headed enough to taste a cup, know what is in it, and refuse it as our Lord did.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'arab (to mix, to be intermingled) carries the covenantal warning; macak (to mix, to mingle wine) the hospitable and the judicial cup; Greek mignumi (to mix) renders the cup at Golgotha.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'arab (H6148) — to mix, intermingle, become surety; the verb of Israel mingled among the heathen.
Hebrew macak (H4537) — to mix or mingle, especially wine; used of Wisdom's prepared table in Proverbs 9:2.
Hebrew mecek (H4538) — a mixture; the cup in the LORD's hand whose wine is red and full of mixture.
Greek mignumi (G3396) — to mix, mingle; used of the vinegar mingled with gall at Matthew 27:34.
Aramaic 'arab (H6151) — to mix, mingle; the verb of Daniel 2:43 for the union that will not cleave.
usage: “Were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works” — mingling precedes and produces imitation.
“They shall not cleave one to another” — some mixtures never bond, however hard they are pressed.
“He would not drink” — our Lord refused what would have dulled His sufferings.

pos: v. (to speak or pronounce; to give forth in words; rendering Hebrew naba, 'amar, Greek laleo, ereugomai)
etymology: From the root of out, to put forth. What is uttered is what has come out; Scripture therefore treats utterance as evidence, since a man's mouth publishes what his heart has been storing.
biblical_def: To utter is to bring into speech what was within, and Scripture uses the word for creation's testimony, the Spirit's intercession, and the fool's self-exposure. The heavens are its first speakers: “Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge” (Psalm 19:2). The utterance is continual and wordless, and the psalm goes on to say that its line is gone out through all the earth, so that no man is without witness. At the other extreme stands a groaning that cannot be brought into speech at all: “the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Romans 8:26). The saint who does not know what he should pray for is not thereby unrepresented; the intercession proceeds above the level of his words. Scripture also weighs utterance as a test of wisdom, and the proverb is blunt: “A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards” (Proverbs 29:11). The mark of folly is not having thoughts but emptying them. Even faithful teachers meet a limit, though the limit lies in the hearers: “Of whom we have many things to say, and hard to be uttered, seeing ye are dull of hearing” (Hebrews 5:11).
webster_summary: To speak; to pronounce; to express in words; to put forth or emit. Scripture uses it of the heavens uttering speech day by day, of groanings the Spirit makes which cannot be uttered, and of the fool who utters all his mind.
webster_full: UTTER, v.t. [from out.] To speak; to pronounce; to express; as, to utter words; to utter a cry.
2. To disclose; to discover; to divulge; to publish; as, to utter a secret.
3. To sell; to vend; to put into circulation, as money or notes.
4. To emit; to send forth; as, a spring utters water.
UTTER, a. Entire; complete; total; as, utter darkness; utter ruin.
2. Extreme; excessive; utmost; as, the utter end. UTTERANCE, n. The act of uttering; pronunciation; manner of speaking.
scriptures: Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge.
Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.
Of whom we have many things to say, and hard to be uttered, seeing ye are dull of hearing.
corruption_summary: The unutterable groanings of Romans 8:26 are regularly claimed as a proof-text for ecstatic speech, though the passage says the groanings are the Spirit's own and cannot be put into words at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Charismatic and New Apostolic teaching commonly reads Romans 8:26 as a description of the believer praying in unintelligible syllables, and builds a practice on it. The text will not support the reading. The groanings belong to the Spirit, not to the worshipper's tongue; they are said to be unutterable, which is the opposite of being uttered audibly; and the comfort offered is precisely for the saint who does not know what to pray and produces no adequate speech at all. The verse is a consolation for inarticulate weakness, and turning it into a technique robs the weak of the only passage addressed to their case.

The corresponding corruption in the pew is the elevation of unrestrained expression as honesty. Proverbs 29:11 calls the man who utters all his mind a fool, and the age calls him authentic. Scripture never commends concealment of sin, and it constantly commends restraint of speech: the wise man keeps it in till afterwards, the tongue is a fire, and every idle word will be accounted for. Recover the distinction between confession, which brings the hidden thing to God and to those wronged, and ventilation, which merely publishes a heart that has not been dealt with.
roots_summary: Hebrew naba (to pour forth, to gush) gives Psalm 19:2 its continual speech; Greek laleo (to speak) and alaletos (unutterable) frame Romans 8:26, and dusermeneutos (hard to interpret) Hebrews 5:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew naba (H5042) — to pour forth, to bubble up, to utter; the day-by-day pouring of speech in Psalm 19:2.
Hebrew 'amar (H559) — to say, to speak, to utter; the ordinary verb of speech throughout the Old Testament.
Greek alaletos (G215) — unutterable, inexpressible; the single word governing the groanings of Romans 8:26.
Greek stenagmos (G4726) — a groaning, a sighing; what the Spirit makes on behalf of the saints.
Greek dusermeneutos (G1421) — hard to interpret or explain; the difficulty in Hebrews 5:11, located in dull hearers.
usage: “Day unto day uttereth speech” — creation testifies continually and without words.
“Groanings which cannot be uttered” — the Spirit's intercession rises above the saint's speech.
“A fool uttereth all his mind” — restraint of speech is a mark of wisdom, not of dishonesty.

pos: v. (to distribute or apportion; to act toward a person; rendering Hebrew gamal, bagad, Greek merizo)
etymology: From Saxon dælan, to divide or distribute. The word keeps both halves in Scripture: to deal is to hand out bread, and to deal is to conduct oneself toward another — bountifully, or treacherously.
biblical_def: Deal in the Authorized Version carries two senses that Scripture keeps close together: to distribute a thing, and to conduct oneself toward a person. Isaiah puts the first at the head of the fast God chooses: “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?” (Isaiah 58:7). The bread is thy bread, dealt out by the hand that owns it, and the last clause forbids the convenient blindness that gives to strangers while ignoring kin. The second sense is covenantal and can be violated: “Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, by profaning the covenant of our fathers?” (Malachi 2:10). Treachery between brothers is treated as a profaning of the covenant, not merely as a private wrong. Against both stands the way God deals with His own, which is stated first negatively — “He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 103:10) — and then positively, as the ground of song: “I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me” (Psalm 13:6).
webster_summary: To divide; to distribute; to give out in portions; also, to conduct oneself toward another, well or ill. Scripture commands dealing bread to the hungry, forbids dealing treacherously with a brother, and grounds praise in God's bountiful dealing with sinners.
webster_full: DEAL, v.t. [Sax. dælan, to divide.] To divide; to part; to separate; hence, to divide in portions; to distribute; as, to deal out bread to the poor.
2. To scatter; to throw about; as, to deal blows among the enemy.
3. To distribute the cards of a pack to the players.
DEAL, v.i. To traffick; to trade; to negotiate; as, to deal in silks.
2. To act between man and man; to intervene; to behave well or ill; as, to deal justly with all men.
DEAL, n. A part or portion; a distribution; also, an indefinite quantity or degree; as, a great deal of time.
scriptures: Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?
Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, by profaning the covenant of our fathers?
He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities.
I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 58 has been enlisted for a politics of redistribution, so that the personal duty of dealing one's own bread to the hungry is transferred to the state and the man himself is excused from the fast God chose.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 58:7 is among the most quoted texts in progressive religion, and the quotation nearly always drops the possessive. The prophet says thy bread, and the acts he lists are all personal and costly: bringing the poor that are cast out into thy house, covering the naked thou seest, refusing to hide from thine own flesh. Transfer the duty to an agency and every element of the fast disappears — the bread is no longer the giver's, the poor man never enters his house, and the giver never sees the naked he covers. The chapter is a rebuke of religious performance, and administering a policy is a performance available to a man whose own door stays shut. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: names the redistributive reading of Isaiah 58 in order to rebut it

The opposite corruption seizes on that argument to evade the text altogether, treating Isaiah 58 as ancient ceremony and mercy to the poor as optional. Scripture forecloses that too. The fast God chooses is defined by these acts, Malachi ties dealing treacherously with a brother to profaning the covenant, and the whole is bounded by how God deals with us — not after our sins, but bountifully. A people dealt with on that principle and refusing to deal so with others has misunderstood the mercy it claims.
roots_summary: Hebrew gamal (to deal out, to recompense) gives Psalm 13:6 its bounty; bagad (to act treacherously) gives Malachi 2:10 its charge; Greek merizo (to divide, apportion) carries the distributive sense.
roots_lines: Hebrew gamal (H1580) — to deal out, to recompense, to wean; the verb behind “he hath dealt bountifully with me”.
Hebrew bagad (H898) — to act treacherously, to deal falsely; the repeated charge of Malachi 2.
Hebrew parac (H6536) — to break in pieces, to break bread; the breaking implied in dealing bread to the hungry.
Greek merizo (G3307) — to divide, to distribute in portions; the New Testament counterpart of the distributive sense.
Greek koinoneo (G2841) — to share, to communicate; the apostolic word for the same duty of distribution.
usage: “Deal thy bread to the hungry” — the bread is the giver's own and the giving is personal.
“Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother?” — treachery among brethren profanes the covenant.
“He hath not dealt with us after our sins” — God's dealing is the measure of ours.

pos: v. (to keep fast; to retain in the grasp; rendering Hebrew tamak, chazaq, Greek krateo, katecho)
etymology: From Saxon healdan, to keep or retain. The Christian's holding fast is real and commanded, and it rests underneath on a prior holding — the hand that holds him was not the one he took hold of first.
biblical_def: To hold is to keep in the grasp, and Scripture puts the word on both sides of the believer's security. Underneath everything is God's holding: “Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand” (Psalm 73:23). Asaph says it after admitting that his feet were almost gone and his steps had well nigh slipped, so the holding is what accounts for a man who nearly fell and did not. Upon that ground the commands to hold fast are laid, and they are genuine commands: “Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession” (Hebrews 4:14). The reason given for holding is not the strength of the grip but the greatness of the Priest. The risen Christ presses the same duty on a church under pressure, with a warning attached: “Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown” (Revelation 3:11). What is held may be taken by another's hand if it is let go. And the word turns outward in Paul, where holding becomes displaying: “Holding forth the word of life; that I may rejoice in the day of Christ, that I have not run in vain” (Philippians 2:16).
webster_summary: To keep fast; to retain in the grasp; to maintain, defend, or possess; to restrain. Scripture grounds the believer's holding fast upon God's prior holding of him by the right hand, and commands both retention of the faith and its holding forth to others.
webster_full: HOLD, v.t. [Sax. healdan, to keep, retain.] To stop; to confine; to restrain from escape; to keep fast; to retain.
2. To embrace and confine, with any degree of force; to grasp.
3. To maintain, as an opinion; as, to hold a doctrine to be true.
4. To possess; to keep; to occupy; as, to hold an estate or an office.
5. To consider; to regard; to esteem; as, to hold a man in honor.
HOLD, v.i. To be true; not to fail; as, the argument holds. To continue unbroken or unsubdued; to adhere; to cling. HOLD, n. A grasp; a seizing; a fort or stronghold.
scriptures: Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand.
Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.
Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.
Holding forth the word of life; that I may rejoice in the day of Christ, that I have not run in vain, neither laboured in vain.
corruption_summary: Holding fast has been recast as rigidity, and the abandonment of received doctrine — renamed deconstruction — is presented as a stage of growth rather than as the letting go Scripture warns against.
corruption_paragraphs: The vocabulary of deconstruction has given the age a respectable name for apostasy's early stages. A man is taught that dismantling what he was given is the mark of an examined faith, and that holding what he received is the mark of a mind that has not yet begun to think. Revelation 3:11 addresses a congregation with little strength that had kept Christ's word, and its command is the reverse: hold that fast which thou hast. Examination is commanded elsewhere, and it is examination by the Scriptures, as the Bereans examined; it is never the progressive dismantling of the deposit itself, which the Apostles call the good thing committed and charge Timothy to keep. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: names deconstruction by its own term in order to rebut it

The opposite corruption misreads the security of Psalm 73:23 as a reason to stop holding at all, on the ground that God's grip makes the believer's grip unnecessary. Scripture joins what that logic separates. The same books that promise no man shall pluck the sheep out of the Father's hand command the sheep to hold fast, endure, and watch, because perseverance is the means by which preservation is worked out. The commands are not a second and rival ground of safety; they are the shape a preserved life actually takes, which is why Asaph's testimony and Hebrews' imperative belong in the same doctrine.
roots_summary: Hebrew tamak (to grasp, uphold) and chazaq (to be strong, to seize) supply the Old Testament sense of upholding; Greek krateo (to seize, hold fast) and katecho (to hold down, retain) carry the New Testament commands.
roots_lines: Hebrew tamak (H8551) — to grasp, to hold up, to support; the LORD holding Asaph by the right hand.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to seize, to hold fast; used of strengthening the hands and of taking firm hold.
Greek krateo (G2902) — to be strong, to seize, to hold fast; the command of Revelation 3:11.
Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold down, to retain, to keep in memory; used of holding fast the word preached.
Greek epecho (G1907) — to hold forth, to give attention to; the verb of Philippians 2:16 for holding forth the word of life.
usage: “Thou hast holden me by my right hand” — the believer's grip rests on a prior grip.
“Let us hold fast our profession” — the reason offered is the greatness of the High Priest.
“Hold that fast which thou hast” — what is let go may be taken by another.
